L49: cite6†Image: Spark icon L50: ## Page Summary

L52: outlined_flag
L53: 
L54:   * MedGemma is a collection of Gemma 3 variants trained for performance on medical text and image comprehension to accelerate the building of healthcare-based AI applications.
L55: 
L56:   * MedGemma comes in a 4B multimodal version, a 27B text-only version, and a 27B multimodal version, with multimodal versions utilizing a SigLIP image encoder trained on de-identified medical data.
L57:   * MedGemma variants have been evaluated on clinically relevant benchmarks for baseline performance, and developers can fine-tune them for improved performance.
L58: 
L59:   * MedGemma is optimized for medical applications involving text generation, while MedSigLIP is recommended for medical image-based applications without text generation.
L60:   * The use of MedGemma is governed by the Health AI Developer Foundations terms of use, and the models were trained on a combination of public and licensed de-identified datasets.
L61: 
L62: Note: This card describes MedGemma 1.5, which is only available as a 4B multimodal instruction-tuned variant. For information on MedGemma 1 variants, refer to the cite7†MedGemma 1 model card .

L77: ## Model information
L78: 
L79: This section describes the specifications and recommended use of the MedGemma model.
L80: ### Description
L81: 
L82: MedGemma is a collection of cite21†Gemma 3†ai.google.dev variants that are trained for performance on medical text and image comprehension. Developers can use MedGemma to accelerate building healthcare-based AI applications.
L83: 
L84: MedGemma 1.5 4B is an updated version of the MedGemma 1 4B model.
L85: 
L86: MedGemma 1.5 4B expands support for several new medical imaging and data processing applications, including:
L87:   * High-dimensional medical imaging: Interpretation of three-dimensional volume representations of Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
L88:   * Whole-slide histopathology imaging (WSI): Simultaneous interpretation of multiple patches from a whole slide histopathology image as input.
L89:   * Longitudinal medical imaging: Interpretation of chest X-rays in the context of prior images (e.g., comparing current versus historical scans).
L90:   * Anatomical localization: Bounding box–based localization of anatomical features and findings in chest X-rays.
L91:   * Medical document understanding: Extraction of structured data, such as values and units, from unstructured medical lab reports.
L92:   * Electronic Health Record (EHR) understanding: Interpretation of text-based EHR data.
L93: In addition to these new features, MedGemma 1.5 4B delivers improved accuracy on medical text reasoning and modest improvement on standard 2D image interpretation compared to MedGemma 1 4B.
L94: MedGemma utilizes a cite22†SigLIP†arxiv.org image encoder that has been specifically pre-trained on a variety of de-identified medical data, including chest X-rays, dermatology images, ophthalmology images, and histopathology slides.
L95: The LLM component is trained on a diverse set of medical data, including medical text, medical question-answer pairs, FHIR-based electronic health record data, 2D and 3D radiology images, histopathology images, ophthalmology images, dermatology images, and lab reports for document understanding.
L96: MedGemma 1.5 4B has been evaluated on a range of clinically relevant benchmarks to illustrate its baseline performance. These evaluations are based on both open benchmark datasets and internally curated datasets. Developers are expected to fine-tune MedGemma for improved performance on their use case. Consult the cite23†Intended use section for more details.
L97: MedGemma is optimized for medical applications that involve a text generation component. For medical image-based applications that do not involve text generation, such as data-efficient classification, zero-shot classification, or content-based or semantic image retrieval, the cite24†MedSigLIP image encoder is recommended. MedSigLIP is based on the same image encoder that powers MedGemma 1 and MedGemma 1.5.
L98: ### How to use
L99: 
L100: The following are some example code snippets to help you quickly get started running the model locally on GPU.
L101: Note: If you need to use the model at scale, we recommend creating a production version using cite9†Model Garden†console.cloud.google.com . Model Garden provides various deployment options and tutorial notebooks, including specialized server-side image processing options for efficiently handling large medical images: Whole Slide Digital Pathology (WSI) or volumetric scans (CT/MRI) stored in cite25†Cloud DICOM Store†docs.cloud.google.com or cite26†Google Cloud Storage (GCS)†cloud.google.com .
L102: First, install the Transformers library. Gemma 3 is supported starting from transformers 4.50.0.
L103: 
L104:     `$ pip install -U transformers
L105:     `
L106: 
L107: Next, use either the pipeline wrapper or the transformer API directly to send a chest X-ray image and a question to the model.
L108: 
L109: Note that CT, MRI and whole-slide histopathology images require some pre-processing; see the cite27†CT†github.com and cite28†WSI†github.com notebook for examples.
L110: Run model with the pipeline API
L111: 
L112:     `from transformers import pipeline
L113:     from PIL import Image
L114:     import requests
L115:     import torch
L116: 
L117:     pipe = pipeline(
L118:         "image-text-to-text",
L119:         model="google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it",
L120:         torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
L121:         device="cuda",
L122:     )
L123: 
L124:     # Image attribution: Stillwaterising, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
L125:     image_url = "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c8/Chest_Xray_PA_3-8-2010.png"
L126:     image = Image.open(requests.get(image_url, headers={"User-Agent": "example"}, stream=True).raw)
L127: 
L128:     messages = [
L129:         {
L130:             "role": "user",
L131:             "content": [
L132:                 {"type": "image", "image": image},
L133:                 {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this X-ray"}
L134:             ]
L135:         }
L136:     ]
L137: 
L138:     output = pipe(text=messages, max_new_tokens=2000)
L139:     print(output[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])
L140:     `
L141: Run the model directly
L142: 
L143:     `# Make sure to install the accelerate library first via `pip install accelerate`
L144:     from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForImageTextToText
L145:     from PIL import Image
L146:     import requests
L147:     import torch
L148: 
L149:     model_id = "google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it"
L150: 
L151:     model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
L152:         model_id,
L153:         torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
L154:         device_map="auto",
L155:     )
L156:     processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
L157:     # Image attribution: Stillwaterising, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
L158:     image_url = "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c8/Chest_Xray_PA_3-8-2010.png"
L159:     image = Image.open(requests.get(image_url, headers={"User-Agent": "example"}, stream=True).raw)
L160: 
L161:     messages = [
L162:         {
L163:             "role": "user",
L164:             "content": [
L165:                 {"type": "image", "image": image},
L166:                 {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this X-ray"}
L167:             ]
L168:         }
L169:     ]
L170:     inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
L171:         messages, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True,
L172:         return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt"
L173:     ).to(model.device, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
L174: 
L175:     input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
L176: 
L177:     with torch.inference_mode():
L178:         generation = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000, do_sample=False)
L179:         generation = generation[0][input_len:]
L180: 
L181:     decoded = processor.decode(generation, skip_special_tokens=True)
L182:     print(decoded)
L183:     `
L184: ### Examples
L185: 
L186: Refer to the growing collection of cite13†tutorial notebooks†github.com to see how to use or fine-tune MedGemma.
L187: 
L188: ### Model architecture overview
L189: 
L190: The MedGemma model is built based on cite29†Gemma 3†ai.google.dev and uses the same decoder-only transformer architecture as Gemma 3. To read more about the architecture, consult the Gemma 3 cite30†model card†ai.google.dev .
L191: ### Technical specifications
L192: 
L193:   * Model type: Decoder-only Transformer architecture, see the cite31†Gemma 3 Technical Report†storage.googleapis.com L194:   * Input modalities: Text, vision (multimodal)
L195:   * Output modality: Text only
L196:   * Attention mechanism: Grouped-query attention (GQA)
L197:   * Context length: Supports long context, at least 128K tokens
L198:   * Key publication: cite32†https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05081†arxiv.org L199:   * Model created: 4B multimodal: Jan 13, 2026
L200:   * Model version: 4B multimodal: 1.5.0
L201: ### Citation
L202: When using this model, please cite: Sellergren et al. "MedGemma 1.5 Technical Report." arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05081 (2026).
L203: 
L204:     `@article{sellergren2026medgemmatechnicalreport,
L205:       title={MedGemma 1.5 Technical Report},
L206:       author={Sellergren, Andrew and Gao, Chufan and Mahvar, Fereshteh and Kohlberger, Timo and Jamil, Fayaz and Traverse, Madeleine and Tono, Alberto and Sadjad, Bashir and Yang, Lin and others},
L207:       journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05081},
L208:       year={2026}
L209:     }
L210:     `
L211: ### Inputs and outputs
L212: 
L213: Input:
L214: 
L215:   * Text string, such as a question or prompt
L216:   * Images, normalized to 896 x 896 resolution and encoded to 256 tokens each
L217:   * Total input length of 128K tokens
L218: 
L219: Output:
L220: 
L221:   * Generated text in response to the input, such as an answer to a question, analysis of image content, or a summary of a document
L222:   * Total output length of 8192 tokens
L223: ### Performance and evaluations
L224: 
L225: MedGemma was evaluated across a range of different multimodal classification, report generation, visual question answering, and text-based tasks.
L226:

L310: ### Ethics and safety evaluation
L311: #### Evaluation approach
L312: 
L313: Our evaluation methods include structured evaluations and internal red-teaming testing of relevant content policies. Red-teaming was conducted by a number of different teams, each with different goals and human evaluation metrics. These models were evaluated against a number of different categories relevant to ethics and safety, including:
L314:   * Child safety: Evaluation of text-to-text and image-to-text prompts covering child safety policies, including child sexual abuse and exploitation.
L315:   * Content safety: Evaluation of text-to-text and image-to-text prompts covering safety policies, including harassment, violence and gore, and hate speech.
L316:   * Representational harms: Evaluation of text-to-text and image-to-text prompts covering safety policies, including bias, stereotyping, and harmful associations or inaccuracies.
L317:   * General medical harms: Evaluation of text-to-text and image-to-text prompts covering safety policies, including information quality and potentially harmful responses or inaccuracies.
L318: In addition to development level evaluations, we conduct "assurance evaluations" which are our "arms-length" internal evaluations for responsibility governance decision making. They are conducted separately from the model development team and inform decision making about release. High-level findings are fed back to the model team but prompt sets are held out to prevent overfitting and preserve the results' ability to inform decision making.
L319: Notable assurance evaluation results are reported to our Responsibility & Safety Council as part of release review.
L320: #### Evaluation results
L321: 
L322: For all areas of safety testing, we saw safe levels of performance across the categories of child safety, content safety, and representational harms compared to previous Gemma models. All testing was conducted without safety filters to evaluate the model capabilities and behaviors. For both text-to-text and image-to-text the model produced minimal policy violations. A limitation of our evaluations was that they included primarily English language prompts.
L323: 
L324: ## Data card
L325: ### Dataset overview
L326: #### Training
L327: The base Gemma models are pre-trained on a large corpus of text and code data. MedGemma multimodal variants utilize a cite22†SigLIP†arxiv.org image encoder that has been specifically pre-trained on a variety of de-identified medical data, including radiology images, histopathology images, ophthalmology images, and dermatology images.
L328: Their LLM component is trained on a diverse set of medical data, including medical text, medical question-answer pairs, FHIR-based electronic health record data (27B multimodal only), radiology images, histopathology patches, ophthalmology images, and dermatology images.
L329: #### Evaluation
L330: 
L331: MedGemma models have been evaluated on a comprehensive set of clinically relevant benchmarks across multiple datasets, tasks and modalities. These benchmarks include both open and internal datasets.
L332: #### Source
L333: 
L334: MedGemma utilizes a combination of public and private datasets.
L335: This model was trained on diverse public datasets including MIMIC-CXR (chest X-rays and reports), ChestImaGenome: Set of bounding boxes linking image findings with anatomical regions for MIMIC-CXR SLAKE (multimodal medical images and questions), PAD-UFES-20 (skin lesion images and data), SCIN (dermatology images), TCGA (cancer genomics data), CAMELYON (lymph node histopathology images), PMC-OA (biomedical literature with images), and Mendeley Digital Knee X-Ray (knee X-rays).
L336: Additionally, multiple diverse proprietary datasets were licensed and incorporated (described next).
L337: ### Data ownership and documentation
